title: A Horizon for the Protocol
premise: August Almeida, a terraformer hauling seed-cargo through contested orbits around the colony world Vesperin, intercepts the Meridian, a deep-space vessel returned after forty years with its crew aged backward into their twenties, carrying a protocol that can end the war between the colonies and Earth's Directorate. The message is not a weapon but an inheritance: proof that both sides descend from the same sabotaged first fleet, and that the war was engineered to hide it. Pursued by Directorate hunters and colony zealots alike, August must carry the protocol to the neutral relay at Horizon Station before the next offensive launches. In the end, August broadcasts the truth at the cost of their own ship and nearly their life, and the war stalls — not into peace, but into something harder: two peoples forced to remember what they were made to forget.
about_author: Jude Oyelaran is a former agricultural engineer who spent six years designing closed-loop habitats before turning to fiction full-time. Their work explores how ordinary people carry enormous histories in small, practical hands.

chapters.title: Seed Cargo
chapters.summary: August Almeida's POV. A routine haul of soil cultures and embryo vaults through contested orbit establishes August's lonely competence and their quiet devotion to a garden meant for people not yet born. When a distress ping cuts across the shipping lanes, August hesitates — then answers. Emotional beat: duty as habit, loneliness as weather.

chapters.title: The Meridian
chapters.summary: August docks with a derelict-turned-miracle: the Meridian, lost for forty years, its crew young again. Commander Ilsa Reyes, biologically twenty-six but carrying four decades of memory, begs August to take her and her data aboard. Emotional beat: uncanny wonder curdling into dread as August realizes what they've just inherited.

chapters.title: Backward
chapters.summary: Reyes explains the Meridian's time-dilation accident and the protocol hidden in its black box — evidence of the first fleet's shared origin. August's cargo hold becomes an archive. POV shifts briefly to Reyes reliving her crew's deaths in reverse. Emotional beat: grief stretched across impossible time.

chapters.title: Contested Orbit
chapters.summary: A Directorate patrol scans August's freighter. August lies with a terraformer's flat calm while Reyes hides among the seed vaults. The patrol leaves a tracker they don't find until too late. Emotional beat: fear managed through routine, the first taste of being hunted.

chapters.title: What the Garden Is For
chapters.summary: Quiet interlude. August shows Reyes the embryo garden; Reyes, who buried children who are now older than she is, breaks down. They make an uneasy pact: deliver the protocol to Horizon Station's neutral relay. Emotional beat: two kinds of loss recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Colony Zealots
chapters.summary: POV of Dara Okonjo, a colonial militia captain who believes the Meridian is a Directorate trick. She intercepts August demanding the black box as a weapon. August refuses; Dara lets them go — but marks their transponder. Emotional beat: righteousness as its own kind of blindness.

chapters.title: The Tracker
chapters.summary: August discovers the Directorate beacon. Jettisoning it means losing their cargo license and livelihood; keeping it means leading every hunter to Reyes. August jettisons it — and their old life with it. Emotional beat: the price of survival begins coming due.

chapters.title: Dead Drop at Kestrel's Ring
chapters.summary: A smuggler contact offers fuel and fake papers in exchange for a copy of the protocol. August must decide who can be trusted with the truth. The smuggler betrays them within hours. Emotional beat: trust rationed like oxygen.

chapters.title: Reyes's Confession
chapters.summary: Reyes admits the Meridian wasn't lost by accident — her own captain sabotaged the jump to keep the protocol from either side, and she has carried his guilt for forty subjective years. Emotional beat: inheritance as burden, memory as debt.

chapters.title: Hunter
chapters.summary: POV of Directorate agent Corvane, who lost family in the war's first bombardment and wants the protocol destroyed, not read. His pursuit is personal, patient, and merciless. He closes on August's position. Emotional beat: hatred with a human face.

chapters.title: Running Dark
chapters.summary: August kills their transponder and threads an uncharted debris field on manual thrusters, Reyes navigating from forty-year-old charts. The ship barely survives; so does their faith in each other. Emotional beat: terror transformed into intimacy.

chapters.title: The Message Itself
chapters.summary: They finally decrypt the full protocol: genetic and archival proof that colonists and Directorate citizens share the same sabotaged ancestry, and records of who profited from hiding it. The truth is bigger and worse than either hoped. Emotional beat: awe shadowed by futility — will anyone want this?

chapters.title: Ambush at the Relay Approach
chapters.summary: Dara Okonjo's militia and Corvane's Directorate strike team converge on August's ship simultaneously. A three-way firefight in the outer belt; the freighter takes fatal damage. Emotional beat: chaos where every side believes itself the victim.

chapters.title: Abandon Ship
chapters.summary: August seals the embryo garden into an escape pod rather than save themselves, staying behind with the protocol core. Reyes refuses to leave without them. The freighter breaks apart around them. Emotional beat: sacrifice chosen over survival, love over logic.

chapters.title: Drift
chapters.summary: Adrift in a damaged shuttle with failing air, August and Reyes wait. August reflects on the garden they may never see planted. Corvane finds them — and instead of firing, demands to hear the message. Emotional beat: stillness before the storm; an enemy listening.

chapters.title: Corvane's Choice
chapters.summary: Corvane reads the protocol's evidence against his own family's war record and finds his grief was manufactured. He doesn't convert — he simply stops. He gives them his ship's codes and walks into custody. Emotional beat: the war's first casualty is certainty.

chapters.title: Horizon Station
chapters.summary: Using Corvane's codes, August and Reyes reach the neutral relay as the next offensive launches. The station's archivists refuse to broadcast unverified data. August must stake everything on one live transmission. Emotional beat: desperation sharpened into resolve.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Climax. August hijacks the relay and streams the protocol fleet-wide — to colonies, Directorate ships, everyone — narrating it plainly, a terraformer explaining soil and roots. Both fleets' weapons systems hesitate mid-lock. Emotional beat: one small voice making history pause.

chapters.title: Ceasefire, Fragile
chapters.summary: Neither side surrenders; both stand down. Dara Okonjo, watching from her militia ship, orders her people home and resigns. The war doesn't end — it simply stops being inevitable. Emotional beat: exhaustion mistaken for peace, hope held cautiously.

chapters.title: The Cost
chapters.summary: August faces tribunal for piracy and unauthorized broadcast. Reyes testifies; Corvane, in custody, corroborates. August loses their license, their ship, their old name — and gains something stranger: standing. Emotional beat: justice imperfect but honest.

chapters.title: Planting Season
chapters.summary: Years later, August tends the embryo garden on Vesperin's surface, now a public archive and nursery. Children born since the ceasefire play among the vaults. Reyes visits, still younger than her memories. Emotional beat: inheritance fulfilled — memory passed down instead of buried.

chapters.title: A Horizon for the Protocol
chapters.summary: Final chapter, August's voice. Standing at the garden's edge under an unfamiliar sky, August reflects that survival was never free — someone always pays, and the only question is whether the payment buys remembering or forgetting. The horizon holds no promises, only possibility. Emotional beat: hard-won, unsentimental peace.
